name: Chrome nails

card.summary: A mirror-finish nail polish look that gives nails a reflective metallic shine, used as a quick grooming and style upgrade for the hands.

quick.overview:
Chrome nails have a reflective, metallic surface, in silver, gold or tinted shades. The look makes hands look polished and styled, and it has spread through nail salons and social media as a statement finish.

It belongs to the long history of nail colour and the growth of nail art. Wikipedia describes shimmer and metallic effects in polish as coming from ingredients such as mica, bismuth oxychloride, pearl essence and aluminium powder.
quick.how: Chrome is usually applied by a nail technician over a base coat, often with a pigment powder or foil over gel polish, then sealed. Salon visits are repeated as the manicure grows out.
quick.risks: Gel and acrylic systems used for such manicures can cause contact dermatitis in some people, and nail technicians face greater solvent exposure. Some regulators and cities have restricted certain nail-product chemicals.

lead: Chrome nails are a nail finish with a mirror-like metallic surface. They give the nails a reflective shine that can be silver, gold, or coloured, and are worn as a styling and grooming detail for the hands.

The finish sits within the broader history of nail colour, which Wikipedia traces to China around 3000 BCE, with Western use of polish taking off in the 1920s and full-nail painting common by the 1940s [1]. Modern polish is typically a film-forming polymer such as nitrocellulose dissolved in solvent, while gel versions use acrylate polymers cured under UV or LED light [1]. Shimmer and metallic effects in polish are attributed to mica, bismuth oxychloride, pearl essence and aluminium powder [1].

angle.text: Chrome gives an immediate cosmetic change to the nails. The finish lasts until it chips or grows out and is renewed at the salon.

infobox: Metallic pigments; gel systems cured by UV/LED [1]

paras: Polish is composed of a film-forming polymer, solvents, plasticizers, pigments, resins and thickeners, and gel polish cures under lamps [1]. Nail art has grown with social media; U.S. nail-polish sales reached $768 million in 2012, a 32 percent increase over 2011, and the 2020s have brought magnetic polish, stickers and colour-changing formulas [1].

Health risks of nail products are debated: some regulators regard typical consumer exposure as low, while technicians have higher solvent exposure. Methyl methacrylate and HEMA in gel products have caused dermatitis and respiratory concerns, and have been banned in Europe or restricted to professional use in parts of the U.S. [1]
